title: Ukraine Drones Hit Turkish Ships in Black Sea, Framework Law Gathers Signatures, Inflation's Mixed Signal
subhead: A Ukrainian drone attack on two Turkish-owned cargo vessels near Novorossiysk forced Ankara to demand Black Sea safety guarantees, while the Kurdish peace framework bill secured cross-party signatures ahead of parliament's summer recess, and July inflation data showed core pressures easing even as fuel costs climb.

sections.heading: Black Sea: Ukrainian Drones Strike Turkish-Owned Vessels
sections.body:
Two Turkish-linked cargo ships were hit by drone attacks in the Black Sea late Monday, seriously injuring three Turkish crew members and forcing Ankara to issue an urgent call for Russia and Ukraine to ensure navigational safety.

According to Turkey's Foreign Ministry, the Cameroon-flagged Ro-Ro vessel Nadezhda was attacked roughly 37 km off Russia's Novorossiysk port while sailing from Samsun carrying fresh produce. Captain Yalçın Şahin reported six or seven drones targeted the vessel, causing a fire and wounding four crew — three of them Turkish nationals. A second Turkish-owned ship, the Yasar, sailing under the Panamanian flag, was also struck the same evening, the ministry confirmed.

Turkey's Foreign Ministry said it was 'deeply concerned about the escalating conflict between Russia and Ukraine in the Black Sea, which is affecting civilian shipping despite all of our warnings,' and urged all parties to 'urgently implement concrete measures to ensure the safety of navigation.' The ministry warned that unless preventive steps are taken, 'the escalation in the Black Sea will have multifaceted negative repercussions, including for food security.'

The incidents come as NATO allies Romania, Bulgaria, and Turkey recently expanded a joint mission to safeguard commercial shipping and clear drifting mines in the Black Sea. Ukraine has escalated strikes on vessels it says support Russia's military logistics, targeting Russian-flagged and Russia-bound ships in both the Black Sea and Sea of Azov.
sections.whyItMatters: This is the second time in months that Turkish shipping has been caught in the Russia-Ukraine crossfire in the Black Sea. It tests Ankara's ability to protect its commercial fleet and its credibility as a neutral mediator — while also underscoring that the war's disruption of grain and trade routes directly threatens Turkey's economic interests.

sections.heading: Kurdish Peace Process: Framework Bill Secures Cross-Party Signatures
sections.body:
The 'Terror-Free Turkey' framework bill — officially titled the Law on Strengthening National Solidarity and Social Cohesion — advanced significantly as parliamentary leaders signed onto the 12-article draft before the TBMM adjourned for its summer recess on Tuesday.

MHP leader Devlet Bahçeli became the first party leader to sign the bill, joined by MHP officials Feti Yıldız, Celal Adan, Erkan Akçay, and Filiz Kılıç. The signing process was opened in the AK Party group as well. TBMM Speaker Numan Kurtulmuş also signed the bill. The draft is expected to be submitted to the parliament with the joint signatures of AK Party, MHP, and DEM Party.

According to details reported by Haberler.com, the bill is not a general amnesty and does not grant any legal status to Abdullah Öcalan. PKK members seeking to benefit must apply within six months. Crimes committed before 2005 carrying aggravated life or life sentences are excluded. For other sentences, a deferral-then-reduction formula applies: sentences under 15 years are deferred for 5 years, those over 15 years for 10 years, after which convictions are dropped if no violations occur.

DEM Party co-chair Tuncer Bakırhan called the bill 'the first step of crossing a historic threshold through law,' urging that 'August should be the month when the foundations of peace are laid, and October should be a spring month for building democratic Turkey.' He also called for the establishment of a Peace Monitoring Committee in parliament with participation from all parties, and a roadmap for democratic and legal reforms in the fall.
sections.whyItMatters: The cross-party signing of the framework bill before recess is a tangible step forward in a process that has been mostly rhetorical until now. But the real test comes after October 1 when parliament reconvenes: the bill must pass through the Justice Commission and a General Assembly vote, and DEM Party's demand for broader democratic reforms — on language rights, local governance, and trustee appointments — will test the coalition's cohesion.

sections.heading: Inflation: Core Pressures Ease, Fuel Costs Climb
sections.body:
The TCMB's July price developments report confirmed annual inflation fell to 31.75%, down 0.36 percentage points from June, with monthly consumer prices rising 1.78%. The central bank said the underlying trend in inflation moderated compared to the previous month.

The picture is mixed. Core goods prices fell 0.38% monthly — the first decline in months — driven by seasonal clothing discounts and weakening durable goods inflation. Processed food inflation also slowed. But service prices rose 3.18% monthly, pushed up by a 16.41% jump in healthcare costs from an SGK co-pay adjustment (which alone added 0.22 percentage points to headline inflation) and rising transport costs reflecting higher fuel prices.

Fuel prices are the clearest upward pressure: the TCMB noted that rising crude oil prices and the gradual exit from the 'esel mobil' (sliding-scale tax) system are pushing pump prices higher. Energy was the primary driver of monthly inflation alongside services.

Separately, the TCMB reported that the CPI-based real effective exchange rate index rose to 105.96 in July, up 0.39 points — meaning the lira's real value appreciated modestly, driven by domestic inflation outpacing nominal currency depreciation. The USD appreciated 1.76% against the lira on average in July, while the euro gained 0.77%.
sections.whyItMatters: The moderation in core inflation is encouraging for the TCMB, but the fuel-driven upside from the Iran-Hormuz conflict and the healthcare one-off make the September rate decision a close call. International banks are split: BBVA and Goldman see year-end inflation at 29-30%, while Citi expects 31.8%. The central bank held rates at 37% in July and publishes its next inflation report on August 13.

sections.heading: HSBC Report: Easing Delayed, Not Derailed — With Risks
sections.body:
HSBC Global Investment Research published its 'Anatolian Adaptation' report on August 4, maintaining a positive structural view on Turkish equities while acknowledging near-term headwinds. Turkish stocks have outperformed the FTSE Emerging Markets index by 5 percentage points year-to-date, but most gains came in January-February, with the market range-trading since the Iran conflict began.

The report highlighted that rising oil prices have pushed up inflation expectations and forced the TCMB to keep its one-week repo rate at 37%, delaying monetary easing. However, HSBC economists believe that if domestic conditions remain supportive, a rate-cutting cycle could begin in September, with a sustained rally expected from Q4 2026 onward.

Foreign investors pulled roughly $2 billion from Borsa Istanbul after the US-Iran war began, and the foreign share of the market has fallen from 65% to 33% over the past decade. HSBC sees low positioning and attractive multiples — BIST's 12-month forward P/E ratio at 7.5x — as supportive of a long-term recovery, while flagging domestic political uncertainty (including early election speculation) and the MSCI's November review as risk factors.

HSBC identified four structural growth themes: defense industry (rising global military spending and Turkey's growing export share), infrastructure and reconstruction (Levant rebuilding, GCC mega-projects, Ukraine opportunities), AI infrastructure (Turkish transformer and substation suppliers benefiting from US bottlenecks), and aviation (Istanbul gaining market share from Gulf carriers' rerouting).
sections.whyItMatters: The HSBC report crystallizes the tension in Turkey's macro outlook: structural opportunity is real, but the Iran conflict and domestic politics are keeping foreign money on the sidelines. The $2 billion outflow is manageable given low foreign positioning, but any escalation in Hormuz or early election noise could delay the September easing window that markets are pricing in.

sections.heading: Parliament Adjourns Until October as Legislative Clock Pauses
sections.body:
Türkiye Büyük Millet Meclisi (TBMM) entered its summer recess on Tuesday, with the assembly not scheduled to reconvene until October 1. The framework bill's advance before recess means the Justice Commission will take it up when parliament returns, with the General Assembly vote expected by the end of that week at the earliest.

The recess leaves several time-sensitive items in limbo: beyond the framework law's commission and plenary stages, any supplementary democratic reform legislation that DEM Party is demanding — on language rights, local governance, and trustee appointments — will have to wait until fall. The minimum pension differential payments of 23,552 TL are set to be deposited into accounts on August 7.
sections.whyItMatters: Parliament's two-month adjournment means the framework bill's actual legislative passage is weeks away at best. The political momentum built this week risks dissipating over the summer, and any deterioration in the Kurdish peace process on the ground — particularly in northern Syria or Iraq — could harden positions before October.

sections.heading: Hormuz Diplomacy Pushes Oil Below $90, But Shipping Risks Persist
sections.body:
Oil prices dropped sharply on Tuesday — Brent crude fell below $80/barrel at one point — after Qatar said mediators were making progress in efforts to end the US-Iran war, and US officials indicated a Hormuz deal could be reached by mid-week. Treasury Secretary Bessent and Secretary of State Rubio both pointed to progress in talks on reopening the strait, which normally carries about a fifth of global oil and LNG shipments.

Iran denied Trump's assertion that negotiations are already underway, though Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson said talks with Oman over safe transit through the strait were 'positive and continuing.' A cargo vessel was struck by an unidentified projectile near Hormuz off Oman's coast, and an Indian-flagged ship was hit and sank near Yemeni waters — reminders that the shipping corridor remains dangerous even as diplomacy advances.

For Turkey, the oil price relief is significant: every $10 drop in Brent saves roughly $3-4 billion in annual import costs. The TCMB's July report already noted that rising crude prices and the phased exit from the sliding-scale fuel tax mechanism were pushing pump prices higher. A sustained sub-$90 Brent would ease pressure on the lira and inflation trajectory ahead of the central bank's August 13 inflation report.

Meanwhile, the Iraq-Syria pipeline bypass of Hormuz continues to gain traction, with Saudi Aramco reporting bumper profits from its use of the East-West pipeline and analysis noting that states from the UAE to Syria are seeking alternatives to the Hormuz chokepoint.
sections.whyItMatters: Turkey is one of the biggest beneficiaries of a Hormuz de-escalation: it imports nearly all its energy, and the conflict-driven price spike has been the single biggest headwind to the TCMB's disinflation program. But a deal to reopen the strait is not yet done, and until shipping lanes are verifiably safe, insurance costs and rerouting premiums will keep energy import bills elevated.

bottomLine: Two Ukrainian drone attacks on Turkish-owned cargo ships near Novorossiysk forced Ankara to demand Black Sea safety measures from Russia and Ukraine — a direct hit on Turkey's commercial shipping interests and its self-image as a neutral mediator. Domestically, the 'Terror-Free Turkey' framework bill gathered cross-party signatures before parliament adjourned until October, but the real legislative work lies ahead. July inflation data showed core pressures easing while fuel costs climb, and HSBC's new report captures the macro tension: structural opportunity is real, but foreign investors need to see the Iran conflict de-escalate and domestic politics stabilize before the September easing window can open. Oil's slide toward $80 on Hormuz diplomacy hopes is the biggest potential tailwind for Turkey right now — if it holds.
